blocks.text: It is a thin-walled 8-10 cm long tube leading from the outside to the cervix of uterus. It provides a passageway for delivery of infant and for menstrual flow.

blocks.alt: Anterior view of the female reproductive organs in section: the pear-shaped uterus with its domed fundus at the top and the uterus body around the central cavity, narrowing into the cervix and the vagina below; an oviduct (fallopian tube) curves out from each upper corner and ends in finger-like fimbriae beside an ovary, which is tied to the uterus by a ligament.
blocks.caption: Figure 17.4: Human female reproductive system (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.4).

blocks.text: The production of ovum starts during the embryonic development of female. In that period, the oogonia (2n) present in follicle divide by mitosis to produce primary oocytes (2n). These primary oocytes begin the first meiotic division, but stop in prophase-I. They remain in prophase-I all through childhood (for at least 10 to 14 years).

blocks.alt: Vertical sequence with time bands. Before birth: oogonium (2n), mitosis, primary oocyte (2n) arrested in meiosis-I. Band: childhood, ovary inactive. From puberty to menopause: primary oocyte (2n), meiosis-I gives a first polar body (n, dies) and a secondary oocyte (n) arrested in metaphase-II; the secondary oocyte is ovulated and met by a sperm; meiosis-II is completed if fertilized, giving a second polar body (n, dies) and the zygote (2n).
blocks.caption: Figure 17.5: Oogenesis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 17.5).

blocks.text: At puberty, only one of the many primary oocytes present in ovary resumes meiosis-I and produces two dissimilar haploid cells. The larger cell is the secondary oocyte (1n) while smaller one is called the first polar body (1n). The secondary oocyte stops division in metaphase-II. It released from the body. If an ovulated secondary oocyte is not fertilized by a sperm, it dies. But, if a sperm fuses with the secondary oocyte, it quickly completes meiosis II (in oviduct). It produces two new cells i.e., one large ovum (1n) and a small second polar body (1n).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints “It released from the body.” At ovulation the secondary oocyte is released from the ovary (the ruptured Graafian follicle) into the oviduct, not from the body.

blocks.title: For Information
blocks.text: At birth, a female’s ovaries contain some 2 million follicles, each with a primary oocyte.
